EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Georgia Power Company is pleased to report in the Seventh Semi-annual Vogtle Construction
Monitoring (“Seventh VCM”) Report that the Vogtle Units 3 and 4 nuclear energy facility
(“Facility”) continues to be well-managed and is progressing toward our goal of providing a safe,
reliable, clean and cost-effective source of electricity that will provide stable prices and improve
Georgia’s neighborhoods and communities for generations to come. We take seriously our
responsibility to make prudent investments on behalf of our customers and to be accountable to
them. Our customers deserve our best, every day. For that reason, we report that:
• Our uncompromising focus is on Safety and Quality.
Focusing on Safety and Quality will ensure this investment improves Georgia’s
communities and neighborhoods for generations to come. There is simply nothing
more important to us.
• We are focused on the long term reliability of the Facility.
We will continue to focus senior executive management attention at every phase of
this process to ensure that the Facility is the most safe and reliable facility possible
during its 60 year operational life. Customers benefit when we take steps to keep the
Facility reliable and efficient.
• The design and construction of this Facility will result in a safe and reliable source
of electricity.
This Westinghouse designed nuclear energy facility is state of the art. It is based on
the proven safety and performance of prior Westinghouse designs and enhances those
designs to improve plant safety and lower life cycle operational costs. It will further
the achievement of both our nation’s goal of energy independence, and our
customers’ goal of a diverse, cost efficient portfolio of electricity sources.
• We are committed to being transparent to our customers and to all Georgians.
Just as our customers depend on us to deliver reliable, affordable energy that is
cleaner and safer, we are committed to making a prudent investment on behalf of our
customers. We continue to support and encourage the work of the Georgia Public
Service Commission’s Independent Construction Monitor, who is a nationally
respected nuclear engineer, and these semi-annual reviews. As such, this filing will
describe and explain the status of this Facility in as much detail as possible with
nothing redacted in this report.
3
• The Engineering, Procurement, and Construction Agreement is working to ensure
the ultimate rate impacts to customers are minimized.
The estimated cost of the original engineering, procurement, and construction
(“EPC”) scope of the Facility is now $92 million less than was projected at the time
of certification. We have worked to spend more efficiently, and we built protections
into the EPC Agreement to insulate our customers from most construction project
risks that they would face under a “time and materials” contract.
• The overall value of the Facility is now greater for our customers than when the
Facility was certified.
The projected total investment of the Facility continues to track approximately 4
percent below the original certified projection. At the time of certification, the
Company assumed an “in-service” date of April 2016 and April 2017 for Units 3 and
4, respectively. In this Seventh VCM Report, the Company is projecting that the “in-
service” dates for the Facility will be no earlier than November 2016 and November
2017 for Units 3 and 4, respectively. Even with those later “in-service” dates, the
projected cost of the Facility remains below the original certified projected cost.
• While a project of this scale always faces challenges, we remain committed to
completing the Facility safely, successfully and in a timely fashion.
• This Facility represents an important investment that is contributing to the
economy of Georgia today, and that will form the basis of a strong and vibrant
economy for the next 60 years.
This Facility will have less impact on customers than was originally assumed at the time of
certification. We expect the levelized capital and operating costs of the Facility, over its 60 year
life, will continue to track below the costs projected when the Facility was originally certified.
This is shown in Figure A. We remain committed to delivering the most value to customers by
building the Facility as safely and efficiently as possible.

As a result of the Georgia Nuclear Energy Financing Act and this Commission’s Certification
Order authorizing Construction Work In Progress (“CWIP”) in rate base, substantially all of the
Facility investment is expected to be included in rate base by the time the Facility goes into
service, thus eliminating significant rate increases at that time.
We currently project that the total impact on customers’ rates will be even less than projected
when the Facility was originally certified. In 2009, when the Commission originally certified the
Facility as the best option for customers, the Facility’s “overnight” cost was expected to raise
customers’ total rates by approximately 12 percent (without CWIP in rate base) and
approximately 9-10 percent (with CWIP in rate base) when it was placed into service. However,
because of the effects of the lower cost of nuclear fuel compared to other forms of generation, we
also expect customer’s total rates will be 2-4 percent lower than they would otherwise be without
the new Facility in service. As a result, we currently estimate the net rate impact to customers
resulting from the Facility being placed in service at approximately 5-8 percent.
We have identified additional customer benefits. Some of those additional benefits have already
been put in place for our customers and are reflected in the above estimates of lifecycle costs and
rate impacts. Specifically, we anticipate customer benefits of approximately $1.0 billion resulting
from (1) including CWIP in rate base, (2) amending the EPC Agreement to lock in low
commodity costs, and (3) capturing the advantages of historically low interest costs. The
Company is also in position to provide up to an additional $1.0 billion of customer benefits
through production tax credits and additional interest savings, including positioning the
Company to take advantage of Department of Energy (“DOE”) loan guarantees. These interest

Georgia Power has a long and proud history of meeting the needs of its customers and the state
of Georgia with safe, reliable and cost-effective electric energy. We have provided the energy
backbone that has fueled our solid economic development over the past hundred years. Georgia
is now among the nation’s leaders in economic growth, and our services have improved lives in
Georgia’s neighborhoods and communities. By 2020, the state of Georgia expects to add more
than one million new residents. That growth will continue well into the future. The Facility will
provide our customers with safe, reliable and cost-effective electricity for generations to come -
it is a substantial investment for the future.
The approach we have taken is working. We are committed to doing our part to ensure the
continued growth of the Georgia economy and the well-being of its citizens. This ability to have
the proper energy infrastructure in place when it is needed is not the result of happenstance or
luck. It is the result of long range planning by the Company and this Commission. The
Commission, through its resource certification and rate case decisions, has maintained the proper
balance between low customer rates and a utility that is financially healthy enough to attract the
capital required to build and maintain the necessary infrastructure.
As this Commission recognizes, the electric industry is among the most capital intensive
industries in the country. The capital required for building and maintaining the electric
generation, transmission and distribution system in Georgia is significant. For instance, Georgia
Power has over $20 billion invested in Georgia today. Moreover, the other utilities in Georgia
also have substantial amounts invested to serve their customers, including investments by
Oglethorpe Power Corporation, the Municipal Electric Authority of Georgia and the City of
Dalton (collectively with Georgia Power, the “Owners”) in the Vogtle Facility. Much of the
current infrastructure was designed, built and put in service by generations before us. They saw
the future needs and invested their capital to ensure that the necessary electric system would be
in place to meet our needs. For Georgia Power, about half of the invested capital is borrowed in
the form of debt and the other half is invested by shareholders, many of whom are individual
shareholders who work or live here in Georgia.
The design and construction of the Facility is a massive undertaking by any measure. It is one of
the largest and most capital intensive infrastructure projects currently underway in the United
States, representing a $14 billion capital investment in Georgia’s economy. Over 5,000 jobs are
being created, with 2,200 workers on the Vogtle site today. The Facility has increased the tax
base of Burke County as well as the state of Georgia and will continue to do so by creating over
800 full-time, highly skilled and highly paid careers, which will have a compounding effect on
the local economy. Georgia’s electricity will continue to have a diverse fuel supply, ensuring that
prices remain stable and cost competitive for many decades to come, thus providing the
foundation for a strong and vibrant economy. As capital intensive as this project is, completing it
still represents net savings of over $5 billion for our customers compared to the next best
alternative over the life of the Facility. Like all major infrastructure projects that were built by
the sacrifice of those who came before us and that we have come to so heavily rely upon, the
6
Facility represents a commitment by the utilities of Georgia, their current customers, the General
Assembly and this Commission to the economic foundation of those who will come after us.

VCM Report and in this Seventh VCM Report. While each of those projected investments varied
from the others, and from the original certified amount, as with the earlier VCM reports, we do
not request a change in the certified amount at this time.

In this filing, the Company requests that this Commission verify and approve all expenditures
made through and including June 30, 2012 as having been made in compliance with the
certificate. Currently, Georgia Power’s estimated share of the total investment of the Facility is
tracking 4 percent below the original projected total investment (See Figure B). It is tracking
slightly over the projected total investment in the Sixth VCM.

Currently, the projected total investment for the Facility is $6.2 billion. It is important to note,
and as shown in Table 1.0, the construction or “overnight” cost of completing the original scope
of the Facility is actually tracking below the expected cost at the time of certification. As is
described in more detail below, the EPC Agreement insulates our customers to a significant
degree from certain types of cost increases that might otherwise have arisen on a project of this
size. That protection is a significant advantage for our customers.
Through the close of the Seventh VCM reporting period, Georgia Power has invested $2.3
billion in the Facility and during this reporting period, several significant milestones were
reached. Evidence of this progress is depicted in the pictures included in the Progress
Photographs section (Photos 1 through 11) and then discussed in more detail in the Status of
Activities section that follows. The total investment to date includes payments made to
Westinghouse Electric Company and Stone & Webster (collectively, the “Contractor”) pursuant
to the EPC Agreement for the design engineers who have worked both at the site and at remote
locations, the craft labor at the site, for commodities such as piping, concrete, cable and steel. It
includes payments to vendors worldwide who are constructing and assembling the many
components that will be sent to the site for installation, and it includes payments made to
Southern Company affiliates for work performed in support of the Facility, including licensing
and oversight. These investments were all prudent and made in accordance with the EPC
Agreement and principles of sound project management. The Company requests that these costs
be verified and approved.
The cost risks to the Facility for its remaining term are principally related to several key factors,
but particularly related to the expanded scope of the project. There is more work to be done.
8
Future increases are likely to be driven by the following items, as further explained in the Status
of Facility Investment section of this report:
• A greater oversight and project management effort by Southern Nuclear Operating
Company largely driven by our commitment to meeting and exceeding the Nuclear
Regulatory Commission’s requirements on Southern Nuclear as the licensee of the
Facility.
• Time related increases.
• Taxes.
• Transmission interconnection increases.
• Modification to the project scope required by the final design control document as it was
proposed by Westinghouse and approved by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
• The impact on the overall project schedule as a result of the delay in finalizing and
securing approval of the necessary design control document from the Nuclear Regulatory
Commission.
• Requirements of the EPC Agreement that affect scope, and work as agreed to by the
Owners and paid to the Contractor.
• Additional backfill work at the project site.
• Additional costs resulting from federal and state governmental mandates that have
nothing to do with the management of the project, such as increased cyber security and
physical security requirements, and changes to the Fitness for Duty program.
Our goal is to build the safest and most reliable facility possible, one that will deliver a reliable
and efficient source of energy for decades to come. We have always aimed to manage the project
well and to ensure that the investments we make during construction and during the life of the
Facility will make the Facility a safe, reliable, clean, fuel diverse and cost-effective source of
generation during its life.
The Company makes no request in this Seventh VCM Report to increase the certified amount or
to formally extend the schedule. Having said that, we recognize that the April 2016 and April
2017 in-service dates are no longer realistically achievable, given the delay in the DCD approval
process. For purposes of this Seventh VCM Report, the Company has utilized a November 2016
and November 2017 in-service date for Units 3 and 4, respectively. We continue with
negotiations and the formal dispute process with the Contractor to resolve the ongoing cost and
schedule disputes. Once those disputes are resolved, the Owners may conclude that the projected
cost should be revised to reflect additional costs – as necessary and prudent – at that time. At
such time, the Company will notify the Construction Monitor, the Staff and this Commission,
and seek an appropriate amendment to the certificate. While negotiations with our Contractor are
ongoing to resolve the target dates, we have asked them to provide us with a six-month look
ahead schedule to ensure accountability on critical project activities. We have confidence in the
latest schedule and are actively working with the Contractor to finalize the Integrated Project
Schedule.
9
In conclusion, construction of the Facility is progressing well. We are on track to build an
advanced Facility that is on the leading edge of technology and safety, and that delivers excellent
value for our customers. There have been very few endeavors of this magnitude in Georgia’s
history. Even so, comparatively few design, construction, cost and schedule issues have arisen so
far. As new challenges arise, which may be expected in a project of this scale, we will be ready
to face them with an unrelenting focus on our customers. The Company is providing and will
continue to provide effective management. The Facility itself will provide tremendous benefits to
Georgians today and for generations to come.
The Company requests that this Commission verify and approve the construction expenditures
incurred during the Seventh VCM reporting period. The Company makes no request to increase
the certified amount or amend the construction schedule.

PROGRESS PHOTOGRAPHS
We refer the reader to the Southern Company website at www.southerncompany.com (click on
the button in the lower right corner titled Vogtle 3&4) for a more complete and up-to-date
overview of the status of the Facility, periodic status reports since the beginning of construction,
a construction time line and additional pictures of the Facility. The following pages contain
photos of the Facility components and construction in progress.
11
Photo 1 – Unit 3 Reactor Vessel
The reactor vessel houses the nuclear fuel assemblies, where heat is transferred to the reactor coolant system water. The collection of
assemblies is called the core.
12
Photo 2 – Unit 3 Steam Generator
The steam generators produce steam that will drive the turbine generator to produce electricity. The reactor coolant water transfers its
heat to the steam generator water through thousands of tubes.
13
Photo 3 – Unit 3 Pressurizer
The pressurizer is used by operators to raise or lower the reactor coolant system pressure by expanding or collapsing a water-steam
bubble.
14
Photo 4 – Unit 3 Accumulator Tank
The accumulator tanks hold 15,000 gallons of water each. The accumulators are available to passively inject water into the core to
provide backup cooling to the reactor.
15
Photo 5 – Unit 3 Low Pressure Turbine Rotor
The low pressure turbine rotor is one of a series of rotors that uses the force of steam to turn the shaft inside the generator to produce
electricity.
16
Photo 6 – Aerial View of the Construction Site
17
Photo 7 – Unit 3 Nuclear Island
The nuclear island is the heart of the AP1000 where the containment vessel will be placed along with auxiliary systems including
pumps, pipes and tanks.
18
Photo 8 – Heavy Lift Derrick
The heavy lift derrick will be used to place 1,000 ton sections of the containment vessels and large structural modules inside each of
the nuclear islands.
19
Photo 9 – Unit 3 Containment Vessel
The containment vessel will be assembled in stages and placed into the nuclear island using the
heavy lift derrick. The containment vessel will hold the AP1000 reactor, the steam generators,
the pressurizer, the reactor coolant pumps and other supporting safety systems.
20
Photo 10 – Unit 3 Turbine Island
The turbine island will house the turbine generator, condensers, pumps and supporting systems.
21
Photo 11 – Module Assembly Building
Structural sub-modules are assembled and welded onsite inside the Module Assembly Building.

STATUS OF THE FACILITY
I. Status of Activities
Construction of the Facility is now more than one third complete. Construction activities are
progressing well and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has issued the first combined
construction and operating licenses (“COLs”). Full safety-related construction has commenced
on the site. Safety-related construction refers to construction of any structures, systems and
components that are relied upon to remain functional in an emergency event to ensure safe
shutdown of the reactor. Receiving the first ever COL and proceeding with full safety-related
construction marks a major milestone for this project.
Erection of major equipment is underway at the site. The Contractor has assembled the heavy lift
derrick, and load testing has begun. The derrick arrived on site via hundreds of truckloads of
parts that were staged and constructed on site. Significant foundation work was required to
accommodate the 585 foot tall structure that has a boom length of 559 feet. This is one of, if not
the largest heavy lift derricks in the world, standing as tall as some Atlanta skyscrapers, and will
be the principal construction crane for the Facility.
The Company is overseeing major construction activities on the Facility site, such as the
assembly of containment vessels by Chicago Bridge and Iron (“CB&I”). Assembly and welding
of the Unit 3 containment vessel bottom head, which forms the bottom head of the containment
vessel, is complete. Assembly of the Unit 4 containment vessel bottom head is ahead of schedule
and over 50 percent complete. The containment vessel is made up of a bottom head, three rings
and a top head. The first ring, which will attach to the bottom head and form part of the vertical
wall of the containment vessel for Unit 3, is approximately 25 percent complete.
The Unit 3 turbine building foundation is over 65 percent complete, has had about 750 tons of
rebar installed and 5,800 cubic yards of concrete poured and is currently on schedule. The Unit 3
cooling tower deep foundation work is complete and about 50,000 cubic yards of concrete have
been poured to make up the Units 3 and 4 cooling tower foundations. The Unit 3 turbine
condenser components arrived from South Korea on January 31, 2012, the first rail delivery at
the site. The remaining condenser components arrived via 28 rail cars and 65 trucks. Work on the
Unit 3 condenser is now about 20 percent complete. Once assembled, the condensers will be set
inside the turbine building by the heavy lift derrick.
Work is also underway on the first components to be assembled in the onsite Module Assembly
Building, which is a building specially designed to allow assembly of the modules upon arrival
on site. Sub-assembly of the first CA20 structural module for Unit 3, which is the auxiliary
building module, has begun, and once assembled, it will be lifted and placed inside the Unit 3
nuclear island where it will house much of the auxiliary systems and associated pumps, pipes and
tanks. The CA20 module is the largest and heaviest module that will be assembled inside the
Module Assembly Building.
Other current site activities include waterproof membrane application in the Unit 4 nuclear
island, grading work for the electrical switch yard, and support building construction. Also, the
23
river water intake structure preparation work has started and is on schedule. The river water
intake work involves construction of a facility that will house pumps to provide cooling water
from the Savannah River and send that water through pipes to the Facility.
Modifications to the Vogtle Units 1 and 2 230-kV and 500-kV switchyards are ongoing and
progressing on schedule. A new 230-kV switchyard for the new units is under construction as
well with foundation, conduit and fencing work completed on schedule. Work is also underway
and on schedule for the 500-kV transmission line that is being built to add the necessary
transmission infrastructure to support the two new units. The 55 mile line begins at the Thomson
Primary Substation southeast of Thomson and ends at the Facility. The route runs through four
counties: Burke, Jefferson, Warren, and McDuffie. Existing transmission line corridors were
utilized over approximately 13 miles of the line route. The acquisition of land rights will involve
approximately 150 property parcels and the new line will require an easement width of 150 feet.
The transmission line must be in service in time to support the new units and is needed to
continue to provide all of our customers with reliable service. Construction is scheduled to start
in 2013 and the procurement process is on schedule and nearly complete.
After receipt of the COLs, which occurred on February 10, 2012, full safety-related work
commenced and our Contractor began to install steel reinforcing bar, or rebar, for the base mat in
the Unit 3 nuclear island in late February. To date, 450 tons of rebar have been installed in the
Unit 3 nuclear island. The Contractor developed a design and began installing floor rebar at the
floor to wall transition; however, in March, the NRC identified that this design was not in
conformity with the Design Control Document (“DCD”). The Company put the installation work
on hold while it communicated with the NRC, and subsequently submitted a License
Amendment Request (“LAR”) as well as a Preliminary Amendment Request (“PAR”) to modify
the rebar design and adjust the concrete strength referenced in the DCD from 4,000 pounds per
square inch (“psi”) to 5,000 psi, which would meet the desired code and DCD requirements. A
“Notice of No Objection” letter was issued by the NRC on August 2, 2012 for the PAR, and
release to restart rebar installation in the affected critical areas was given on August 3, 2012.
Based on our communications with NRC staff, the Company has a high degree of confidence
that the LAR will be approved by the NRC, and first nuclear concrete for Unit 3 is planned to be
poured upon the Company’s receipt of NRC approval of the LAR, which is expected in October
2012.
Taken as a lesson learned, we have undertaken with the Contractor a thorough review of all
previously processed design changes. More than 30,000 design documents have now been
reviewed to ensure the design complies with the DCD and COLs and to identify any issues that
need resolution through a departure, LAR, or design change. The layers of oversight provided by
the Contractor, the Company and the NRC that were put in place for this project are serving their
intended purpose. This event, while challenging, is an example that highlights the advantage of
the Part 52 licensing process. The rigorous oversight provided by the Contractor, the Company,
and the NRC on the front-end of the project minimizes re-work and ultimately large cost
increases for design issues that may occur for an endeavor of this size and complexity.
Engineering activities to complete the design in conformance with the DCD are progressing well,
with more than 95 percent now finished. The plan for issuance of the Certified for Construction
24
(“CFC”) packages is now incorporated into the Integrated Project Schedule, and pursuant to that
plan, all the packages are expected to be issued by the end of December 2013. The plan allows
for at least six months between the issuance of any one CFC package and its construction need
date to support work planning and activity preparation. Our Contractor reports that the CFC
package issuance fully supports their construction needs.
Procurement of major components and bulk commodities continues to be on track. Major pieces
of engineered equipment, such as the reactor vessels, the steam generators and the core makeup
tanks, are being procured all over the world (See Figure D). While on-time delivery of globally
sourced manufactured equipment is often a cause for delay for many major construction projects,
all such equipment currently remains on schedule, a remarkable achievement in light of the
billions of dollars of equipment that is being procured under the EPC Agreement. Our vendor
surveillance organization, which is responsible for oversight of Contractor procurement and
fabrication of major and bulk components, tracks all planned versus actual procurement activities
for major components, and reports that all the major purchase orders have been issued for the
Facility to support fabrication schedules and meet construction needs.
Figure D – Major Component Fabrication
Fabrication activities around the globe are proceeding in a timely way, with most of the major
components well into fabrication and projected for on-time delivery to support the construction
need dates. The Company and Westinghouse continue to monitor the performance of suppliers.
25
At the Doosan facility in South Korea, fabrication activities of the reactor vessel and steam
generator are ongoing, and tube sheet alignment issues with the Unit 3B steam generator have
been repaired. The Unit 3 reactor vessel final acceptance test, which is hydrostatic testing, has
just concluded and tube installation on the Unit 3 steam generators is now done. In all, 10,025
tubes were installed in each generator. The Unit 4 steam generator tube sheet work, which
includes drilling 20,050 holes, is complete for Unit 4B, and underway for Unit 4A. The
Company is confident that Westinghouse and Doosan will continue to properly address typical
fabrication issues as they arise, and we will continue to monitor fabrication progress to ensure
quality standards are met. Deliveries of the reactor vessel and steam generators for both units are
on track and have adequate margin between site delivery dates and construction needs.
Mangiarotti and its sub-suppliers have improved quality performance and, at this time,
fabrication activities of the pressurizer, the accumulator tanks, the passive residual heat removal
heat exchanger and core makeup tanks are progressing and meeting construction schedule
requirements. The hydrostatic testing of the Unit 3A accumulator tank is about to begin now that
the welding is complete. With the Unit 3 pressurizer shell assembly done, the upper and lower
heads are ready to be welded to the shell. Tube installation is complete in the passive residual
heat removal heat exchanger.
The lead reactor coolant pump for the AP1000 design has completed testing successfully in
Pennsylvania by Curtiss-Wright and several internal components of the Unit 3 reactor coolant
pumps are now being manufactured. Tioga supplier, IBF, is in the final stages of fabrication for
the Unit 3 Reactor Coolant Loop piping.
The Company also continues to closely monitor the production issues at the Shaw Modular
Solutions (“SMS”) facility in Lake Charles, Louisiana. As a result of documentation package
reviews that must be completed on the CA20 structural sub-modules, the shipment of these
modules continue to be delayed. While 26 of the 72 sub-modules have already been delivered to
the project site, another 19 sub-modules have been completed and SMS is performing detailed
quality control reviews of the work packages before shipping the completed sub-modules to the
Facility site. SMS and Shaw Nuclear continue to add resources to oversee, prepare and review
the document packages, and SMS has revised procedures in an effort to increase efficiency
during the fabrication process. SMS is considering outsourcing some fabrication work and
shifting scope of some work to the Vogtle site. SMS has made progress in closing gaps related to
timeliness of corrective actions and all audit findings have been closed through June 2012.
Corrective actions resulting from the November 2011 NRC inspection have also been closed.
The NRC performed an Inspections, Tests, Analyses, and Acceptance Criteria (“ITAAC”)
inspection in May at SMS and no violations were issued.
Finally, our state of the art training facility at the site is now complete and in operation. There are
two limited scope simulators being used to train future operators of the units. Because of the
Company’s solid commitment to operating a safe and reliable electric generating facility, the
groundwork for extensive and rigorous training programs for the next generation of nuclear plant
operators has been in progress for years. The Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (“INPO”)
National Nuclear Accrediting Board granted the initial accreditation of the Vogtle Units 3 and 4
Facility operations training programs, which enables reactor operator candidates to apply for
26
NRC licenses to operate the new AP1000 units. The training program was officially
commissioned as a branch member of the National Academy of Nuclear Training. This is the
first new branch established by the academy in 22 years. As of June 2012, 106 licensed operator
candidates are in the training program.
Looking ahead, there are significant activities scheduled for the fall of 2012. The installation of
the Unit 3 nuclear island rebar is expected to be completed, followed by the first concrete pour of
the Unit 3 nuclear island foundation. The turbine building, mud mat and foundation installation
is expected to conclude in the fall of 2012. Structural module assembly for the nuclear island,
cooling tower foundation installation, circulating water piping placement, river water intake
structure construction and switchyard modifications and are ongoing and will continue through
the reporting period. We expect the Unit 3 reactor vessel to arrive on site this fall. Finally,
assembly of the Unit 4 containment vessel bottom head continues and should conclude in the
spring of 2013.
II. Facility Investment Overview
A. Status of Facility Investment
We are committed to building the safest, most technologically advanced, and most cost-effective
nuclear energy facility. As a result, cost projections will change up and down over the life of this
construction period and in the end, we will only be able to recover those costs that the
Commission, acting on the advice of its independent Construction Monitor, agrees are prudently
incurred. The simple fact is that the only costs recovered from our customers over the 60 year
life of this Facility will be those that the Commission approves and determines to be the
appropriate cost of the Facility, regardless of what projections may have been at any particular
point in time. To be clear, this Commission originally certified the Vogtle Facility at a cost of
$6.446 billion. That projected cost was based on a certain set of assumptions, and as those
assumptions change, or as they play out and become facts, the projected cost will change.
In the First VCM Proceeding, the Commission actually reduced the certified amount from the
original $6.446 billion to $6.113 billion to reflect the changed assumption regarding CWIP. The
$6.446 projection was based on the assumption that CWIP would not be included in rate base. As
a result of the Georgia Nuclear Energy Financing Act and the Commission’s Certification Order,
both of which permitted CWIP to be included in rate base, the projected construction financing
cost and, thus, the total investment of the Facility was reduced in recognition of the savings to
customers those decisions allowed.
In the Second through Sixth VCM proceedings, while the projections changed from report to
report, the certified amount did not. It is important to understand the difference between the
certified amount and the projected total investment. The projected total investment is the most
current projection of cost based upon the most current assumptions such as schedule, scope, and
interest rates. As seen in Figure B on page 7, the projected total investment changes in each
VCM cycle. A subset of the projected total investment is the certified cost. The certified cost is
simply that amount that the Commission has determined will be allowed into rates, assuming it is
27
invested prudently. The regulatory framework under which this Facility is being built clearly
provides that the certified amount may change from time to time, as it did in the First VCM. The
certified amount is intended to reflect the presumed prudent investment at a particular point in
time, not to act as a permanently fixed or capped amount regardless of how the assumptions
upon which it was based change over time or regardless of the actual prudent investment.
The original projected total investment and related value to customers was based on a “timeline”
to complete the first-of-a-kind licensing. While the current fleet of nuclear facilities is safe, this
will be the safest nuclear generating facility ever constructed. The cutting edge design of the Unit
3 and 4 Facility was reviewed in detail over several years by the NRC and includes protections
that would withstand a Fukushima-type event, even though a tsunami will not occur at the Vogtle
site.
Our foremost focus during construction is on safety and quality. The NRC licensing of this
technology was a great success for this project and this state. The limited additional time
required to achieve this first-of-a-kind license, and the additional time it may take to construct
this Facility with the commitment to safety and quality our customers deserve, does not diminish
the value to our customers, or the communities and neighborhoods of our state. We will make
decisions regarding any revised schedule that maintain our commitment to safety and quality in
design and construction as our highest and uncompromising priority.
As of this Seventh VCM Report, the estimated total investment of the Facility is approximately
$6.2 billion. This includes a changed assumption about the “in-service” date for Units 3 and 4 to
November 2016 and November 2017, respectively. This new projection is still below the original
projection and still shows a substantial savings to customers over the next best generating
resource and benefits greater than were assumed at the time of certification. While the Company
has reflected its most current projection of the cost to complete the Facility, we do not seek a
change to the certified amount at this time.
When assessing the overall impact on customers, total lifecycle costs - including the Facility
investment - must be considered. Figure A on page 5 shows the comparison of the First through
Seventh VCM periods and how the estimated lifecycle cost per kWh has improved relative to the
original certified projection. When the additional customer benefits we have identified are
included, the impact is even more favorable.

B. EPC Contract Overview
As this Commission is aware, the EPC Agreement is a contract under which the Contractor is
responsible for the design of the Facility, the procurement and purchase of all the required
materials and equipment, and furnishing the labor workforce and management required to
construct the Facility.
As the EPC Agreement was initially structured, a little more than half of the Total Construction
and Capital Costs (exclusive of financing), was subject to escalation using a market-based index
that is well recognized and commonly used in construction. Amendment No. 3 of the EPC
Agreement, which was approved by this Commission in August 2010 as part of the Second VCM
proceeding, replaced the market-based index with a fixed semi-annual escalator for a significant
portion of the EPC costs. As a result of Amendment No. 3, escalation on more than 80 percent of
the cost covered by the EPC Agreement is fixed. And the fixed escalation rate was significantly
lower than what had been forecasted during the certification proceedings. After Amendment No.
3, essentially 100 percent of the EPC costs are either fixed or firm. By shifting more of the EPC
costs from market-based indexes to fixed escalators, the Company was able to reduce
uncertainty, and therefore costs, for our customers.
Because of this structure, the EPC Agreement effectively insulates our customers from some cost
increases that might otherwise have arisen on a project of this size. Customers are isolated from
typical project risks, such as commodity price changes, commodity quantity estimates, craft
availability and productivity of the labor force. Our Contractor has taken the risk for
procurement and timely delivery of materials, assembly of modules and design to construction
interfaces, which are the risks that are most likely to affect the cost of a major project.
i. The Original Scope
The original scope of the EPC Agreement covers the primary obligations of the Contractor (i.e.,
the Contractor’s obligation to design, procure, engineer, permit, construct, assemble, install, test
and complete the Facility). We have broken that down into the construction or “overnight” cost,
which in this instance is the base cost plus agreed to escalation, but does not include construction
schedule financing costs. The cost for that original scope was set at approximately $3.8 billion
(Georgia Power’s share), as described above. Table 1.0 sets out in separate lines the portions of
the EPC price tied to fixed semi-annual escalation, indexed escalation and other fixed
escalations.
ii. Additional Work and Scope Changes
Other than the price change for the original scope due to escalation, the only other price changes
would be those based on change orders in accordance with the EPC Agreement. While the
Contractor took the price risk on the original scope, Owners took the risk of changes to the scope
driven by specified events. The specified compensable change orders are those resulting from (a)
certain specified changes in law or additional requirements imposed on the design of the Facility
in the COL, (b) agreement by the Owners and Contractor, or (c) certain delays in obtaining
required licenses. In those specified situations, if the Contractor is required to do more work and
30
it cost more or took longer, then Owners are required to compensate the Contractor for those
incurred costs. However, in all other situations in which particular work under the EPC
Agreement costs more or takes longer than was contemplated, the Contractor assumed all risk of
cost increases and the Owners have no obligation to compensate the Contractor for those
additional costs.
The EPC Agreement specifies the manner in which disputes are resolved between the Owners
and the Contractor related to the EPC Agreement, including disputes concerning a change order.
The parties are first required to engage in negotiations regarding the dispute. If they are unable to
agree upon a resolution of the matter through such negotiations, the Owners and the Contractor
must then submit the dispute to a mediation process involving a neutral third party. The
mediation process is designed to facilitate negotiations between the parties with the goal of
reaching a settlement agreement acceptable to both parties. However, if the parties are unable to
reach a resolution within 60 days of the commencement of such mediation, either party may elect
to seek relief through either binding arbitration or in a court of law, depending on the amount of
the claim at issue.
The table below sets out the principal change orders that our Contractor has either requested or
that we expect will be subject to a change order request under the EPC Agreement. We have
accepted several as being obligations of the Owners as specified in the EPC Agreement and we
are disputing others in accordance with the dispute resolution process described above.

C. Quality Assurance, Oversight, Operational Readiness, and Regulatory
In addition to payments to the Contractor, there are also Quality Assurance and Oversight costs
to complete the Owners’ scope of work, and to oversee the Contractor, as further detailed in
Section C.i. below. Increased oversight and project management by SNC is largely driven by
NRC requirements on SNC as the licensee of the Facility. These costs result from regulatory
requirements and will certainly benefit our customers over the life of the Facility. These costs are
required investments. This category captures costs that are also Facility costs that are not costs to
design, procure or construct the physical plant. These are investments to ensure operational
32
readiness of the Facility once it is placed in service, taxes, general and administrative costs such
as accounting and legal costs, and transmission interconnection costs. While the original
expected cost for some of these investments may have been low, the costs themselves are
reasonable and prudent in that other more costly expenses might be avoided benefiting customers
for the life of the Facility.
Georgia Power has no higher priority than ensuring the safe, successful completion of the
Facility and the Company has devoted considerable resources to ensure effective oversight and
management of the project. Primary oversight of the Facility at Georgia Power belongs to the
Executive Vice President of Nuclear Development who reports to the CEO. SNC operates as
agent for Georgia Power, utilizing its industry leading expertise to oversee the Facility. By using
our own oversight employees we are able to leverage the full range of expertise available across
Southern Company and enable Georgia Power to provide robust and thorough management of
the Facility.
The Vogtle 3 and 4 Facility Construction organization is responsible for construction monitoring,
project controls, vendor and on-site fabrication oversight, site engineering, component and
system testing, transmission interface and technical training. The Quality Assurance (“QA”) and
Oversight organization is responsible for quality assurance audits, code compliance, quality
assurance surveillances, quality assessments and conducting readiness reviews.
The Company has continually adapted as new challenges become apparent over the course of the
project. In the Fifth VCM, the Company reported on its additional labor costs, focusing, in part
on ensuring sufficient licensing and engineering resources to support SNC’s obligations as the
licensee. One of the biggest adjustments the Company has made is the deployment of additional
resources to satisfy NRC ITAACs included in the DCD and COL. ITAACs are specified
acceptance tests and documentation that must be submitted to the NRC to demonstrate the
Facility is being built in conformity to all relevant requirements. The Company continues to
monitor staffing needs related to ITAACs and to identify the most efficient way to validate and
document all these 800 plus per unit activities.
Georgia Power has responded to performance issues by adapting the scope of its oversight. The
original scope of oversight was focused on overseeing the installation of the components. For
instance, our initial focus in connection with rebar was ensuring sufficient personnel were in the
field to verify the rebar was installed in accordance with the construction drawings. However, we
have learned that at times, it is necessary to “move upstream,” which in this case meant ensuring
that the design drawings complied with the DCD. As the initial phase of an ongoing effort, we
have performed a check of every design document to be used in construction packages over the
next year.
We continue to use our QA program and vendor oversight group to provide appropriate levels of
oversight to major vendors and we continue to apply pressure to the Contractor to ensure that
they are also providing appropriate QA and general oversight. Where it was deemed necessary,
the Company has sent personnel to provide in-shop oversight of vendor activities but these
decisions have been made on a case-by-case basis and the Company has been careful to utilize
oversight resources in a manner commensurate with the specifics of each situation.
33
These examples demonstrate the evolving nature of the Company’s oversight function and the
fact that the Company is continually adapting its oversight structures and function as new
challenges arise.
D. Construction Schedule Financing
Construction Schedule Financing costs are associated with schedule impacts that might result
from the delay in the DCD, delay in production of modules at SMS and delays in the pouring of
first nuclear concrete (to the extent that is not already subsumed in the delay in issuance of the
DCD). Some time related costs have been lower than projected, such as escalation rates and
financing rates. Some time related costs may be higher than projected, such as extended Quality
Assurance, Oversight, Operational Readiness, and Regulatory resulting from the assumed seven
additional months (April to November) on the project and the additional financing costs for those
months. Likewise, those additional financing costs will not materially adversely affect the value
of the Facility to customers as a 60 year generating asset dedicated to providing low cost
electricity.
E. Contingency
Contingency is not shown on Table 1.0 because a “traditional” contingency was not included as
part of the original certified amount. It is rare, if not unique, that a project of this size and
magnitude has no contingency to cover cost pressures that the EPC Agreement itself clearly
contemplated. This is appropriate under our regulatory framework as long it did not suggest the
conclusion or expectation that the Facility might not exceed its original projected cost without a
contingency. That would be an unrealistic expectation and indeed unprecedented for large
infrastructure projects such as this. It is more usual that a project of this size would have a
contingency of between 20 percent and 25 percent. Instead, because Georgia’s Certification Law
provides such, the Company’s expectation was that if the projected cost increased, the
Commission would review those increases on a cost specific basis and decide then whether the
requested cost increases were prudent or not. The Commission also retained the right to verify
and approve the dollars as they were spent regardless of the budget. That provides the
appropriate level of oversight and customer protection without setting the regulatory expectation
that the projected cost might never increase even if the increase is the result of prudently
increased scope or externally imposed costs.
Of all the broad cost categories itemized in Table 1.0, the cost to actually design, procure and
construct the originally anticipated scope to the Facility has proven to be the most stable, and it
will continue to be the most stable given the structure and protection in the EPC Agreement. As
with any construction project, some individual items will exceed their originally projected cost
and some will run below the original projection, but overall, the increases in the projected cost to
complete the Facility have all been the result of prudent and necessary expenses that will result
in a safe, reliable and cost-effective Facility over its 60 year economic life.
34
III. Additional Customer Benefits
Beginning with the Fifth VCM Report, the Company reports the projected 2016 value of
additional customer benefits since original certification. The anticipated cost impact is less than
it was projected to be at the time of certification due to lower than projected commodity costs,
inclusion of CWIP in rate base, production tax credits (“PTCs”) and lower than projected interest
rates, including the beneficial impacts of the DOE loan guarantee. These customer benefits are
currently estimated at approximately $2 billion and are passed to customers as a result of
Commission and Company actions since Certification to increase the value of the Facility.
Summary of Additional Customer Benefits Since Certification ($ million)
Customer Benefits
PTCs Amendment CWIP in Rate Interest
(2016 Value) Total
(100%) No. 3 Base Savings
In Place $184 $333 $600 $1.1 Billion
Potential $730 $200 $0.9 Billion
TOTAL $730 $184 $333 $800 $2 Billion
Production Tax Credits: The Energy Policy Act of 2005 provides PTCs for companies that
begin construction on new nuclear reactors by 2014 and bring them into service by 2021. The
benefit of the PTCs is provided to customers through a reduction in revenue requirements over
an eight year period following the in-service date for each unit. To recognize the uncertainty in
the underlying assumptions behind the PTC calculations, only 50 percent of the expected tax
credits are assumed in the Company’s economic evaluation, discussed in Item 14.
Amendment No. 3: Amendment No. 3, which was approved by the Commission on August 17,
2010, replaced certain index-based adjustments to the purchase price with fixed semi-annual
escalation amounts and resulted in lower than originally estimated commodity costs. The cost
saving benefit will be passed on to customers through a reduction in revenue requirements over
the life of the Facility.
CWIP in Rate Base: The Georgia Nuclear Energy Financing Act and the Commission’s
Certification Order authorize CWIP to be included in rate base. By including financing costs in
rate base during the construction period, customers avoid paying compounded financing costs
and the in-service cost of the Facility is reduced by over $300 million. This is not a present value
number but a calculation of the reduction to the in-service cost.
Interest Savings: These are debt cost savings that result from lower interest rates in the current
rate forecast versus the rates assumed during certification and include potential annual interest
cost savings from the DOE loan guarantee. The majority of these interest savings, approximately
$600 million, have already been realized through debt issuances made through this Seventh
VCM reporting period. Current market rates are below current forecasted rates, so savings could
ultimately be even greater than currently expected. These savings will be passed on to customers
through lower revenue requirements.

2. A description of any cooperative actions between other builders of nuclear units in the

There has been no change in the status of this item since the last reporting period with the

In light of the Duke Energy and Progress Energy merger, Duke Energy remains engaged in
APOG and this change will not impact the common activities previously performed by
NuStart and now addressed through APOG.

SNC and SCE&G continue working cooperatively to implement a standard approach for
meeting new cyber security requirements that apply to the AP1000 as defined in Regulatory
Guide 5.71, “Cyber Security for Programs for Nuclear Facilities.” The first phase of Cyber
Security work including scope identification and procedure development was completed
during this reporting period.
3. An explanation of how the indices used in the EPC contract are tracking.
The index in the EPC Agreement is currently tracking below original estimates on a
cumulative basis. The original certified projected cost included a forecast for this index based
on 5 percent annual escalation. To date, the indexed rates have experienced a 2-3 percent
annual escalation rate. Combining these savings to date with a forecast for future rates based
on July 2010 actual values escalated at 5 percent, the Company forecasts $21 million in
potential savings as compared to certification.
4. Any updated estimate of onsite spent fuel storage costs, including the costs for dry
storage of spent fuel for an extended period of time after shutdown, and any updated
calculation of spent fuel storage costs assuming Yucca Mountain is never available.
There has been no change in the status of this item since the last reporting period.
5. The status of the Company’s loan guarantee application at the Department of Energy
and to the extent that application is granted, then the Company shall also report on the
impact it has or would have on the final expected in-service cost of the units.
During the Seventh VCM reporting period, the Company and the DOE agreed to extend the
conditional commitment period through December 31, 2012 for the loan guarantee. The
receipt of the COLs from the NRC on February 10, 2012 allowed activities to continue in
support of the final approval and issuance of the loan guarantee but the original conditional
commitment made in February 2010 expired three months after the issuance of the COLs.
The extension did not impact any other terms and conditions of the conditional commitment.
39
The Company remains engaged with the DOE in negotiation of definitive agreements,
completion of due diligence by the DOE, and receipt of any necessary regulatory approvals
or conditions as defined in the definitive agreements. In the event that DOE does not issue a
loan guarantee, Congress takes action to rescind the DOE Loan Program, or Georgia Power
determines that the final terms and conditions of the loan guarantees by the DOE are not in
the best interest of its customers, Georgia Power expects to finance the construction of the
Facility through more traditional means such as security issuances and term loans. Should
any of the preceding events occur, Georgia Power requests that the related deferred issuance
costs be reclassified as a regulatory asset and recovered, to the extent they are not refunded,
over a period to be decided in the next base rate proceeding.
The current estimated impact of the DOE loan guarantee on this Facility is reflected in
financing costs in Tables 1.1, 1.1a, and 8.1. The portion of the estimated net benefits of the
loan guarantee that is allocated to the Facility has been reflected in the Total Current Forecast
based on the information available at this time. Additional costs associated with compliance
with applicable federal regulations pertaining to the acceptance of a loan guarantee may be
identified and incorporated at a later date.

The cost estimates provided in Table 9.1 are based upon the best information available at this
time. The Company will continue to closely monitor these issues and revise estimates as
necessary in future reporting periods. Below is a more detailed description of the major
sources of change during this reporting period.
EPC Contract:
EPC Escalation - Increased escalation costs due to a delay in the completion of certain
milestones when assuming CODs in November 2016 and November 2017 for Units 3 and 4,
respectively.
42
EPC Scope Change -
Cyber Security – Transferred from Quality Assurance, Oversight, Operational Readiness
and Regulatory to EPC Scope Change. There is no additional change to the overall
projected cost for Cyber Security activities.
Support Building Changes - Per Exhibit A of the EPC Agreement, the Company
submitted design requirements for the Site Support Buildings to the Contractor. These
costs represent those submitted by the Contractor for compensation for the work that the
Contractor believes to be beyond the scope of work as contemplated by the EPC
agreement.
Fukushima Tier 1 Impacts - Costs associated with activities, such as standard response
preparation and equipment procurement, which are necessary to comply with the NRC’s
Tier 1 Orders related to the earthquake and resulting tsunami near the Fukushima Dai-
ichi Nuclear Plant. The cost estimate is based on the Contractor’s proposal to provide
standard AP1000 fleet technical support responses for AP1000 COL holders.
Simulator Development System (“SDS”) - The SDS will include the hardware and
software necessary to have a simulator development system that is functionally identical
to the two Plant Reference Simulators provided under the existing AP1000 project scope.
The SDS will allow users to build and test simulator initial conditions, maneuver the
plant, and test plant system functionality prior to loading on the AP1000 Plant Reference
Simulator.
Quality Assurance, Oversight and Operational Readiness:
Extension Costs – Represents the Quality Assurance, Oversight, Operational Readiness
and Regulatory cost impact of extending the assumed CODs of Unit 3 and Unit 4 to
November 2016 and November 2017, respectively. Costs include labor, INPO Dues and
NRC Fees.
Labor Related Expenses (Non-extension) – Labor related expenses were adjusted based
on revised projections for employee benefits including employee medical and pension.
Salaries for operators and operators in training were adjusted to be consistent with market
studies.
Legal Fees - The increase in legal fees is due to an increase in projected legal support and
litigation efforts.
China Lessons Learned - This change will provide a Lessons Learned Program to send
Company personnel to China to observe the component, pre-operational and start-up test
phases at Sanmen and Haiyang nuclear plants. This program will allow for
documentation of lessons learned and beneficial practices of the China AP1000 start-up
programs in efforts to prevent or minimize testing delays on the project.
43
Consulting, Auditing and Compliance - Represents costs to execute current advisory and
audit plans for the Facility.
Construction Utilities - Represents a reduction in the estimate for electricity usage and
pricing at the construction site.
Cyber Security – Transferred to EPC Scope Change. There is no additional change to the
overall projected cost for Cyber Security activities.
Unallocated Budgets - This change represents a reduction in the unallocated portion of
the forecast in order to offset certain increases in Quality Assurance, Oversight,
Operational Readiness and Regulatory and EPC Scope Change budgets.
Rail Spur Maintenance - Represents a reduction in the overall cost estimate for rail spur
maintenance.
Ad Valorem - Increased capitalized ad valorem as a result of the change in assumption
for the CODs from April 2016 and April 2017 to November 2016 and November 2017
for Units 3 and 4, respectively.
10. The status of the Company’s combined construction and operating license (COL)
applications at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
As reported in the Sixth VCM Report, the NRC approved the Unit 3 and Unit 4 COLs on
February 9, 2012 and subsequently issued the COLs on February 10, 2012. The issuance of
the nation’s first COLs is a monumental step for Southern Company, Georgia Power, our
partners, the nuclear industry and the state of Georgia.
On February 17, 2012, Petitioners petitioned the D.C. Circuit for judicial review of the
NRC’s decision to issue the Vogtle COLs. Shortly thereafter, on March 16, 2012, the NRC
denied petitioners’ remaining appeal related to their Fukushima-based contention. For
procedural reasons, petitioners withdrew their original D.C. Circuit petition for judicial
review and filed a new petition for judicial review with the D.C. Circuit, challenging the
NRC’s March 16 rejection of petitioners’ contention. This Vogtle-related D.C. Circuit
petition has been consolidated with petitioners’ D.C. Circuit request for judicial review of the
NRC’s AP1000 rulemaking.
On April 16, 2012, the NRC denied petitioners’ request to stay the Vogtle COLs pending the
D.C. Circuit’s review. Petitioners then made substantively the same stay request before the
D.C. Circuit, which the D.C. Circuit denied on July 11, 2012. Westinghouse and SNC along
with the Vogtle Facility Owners have been granted intervenor status in the D.C. Circuit’s
consolidated docket for the AP1000 and Vogtle COL petitions.
On February 28, 2012 (as updated April 10, 2012), an individual submitted a request for
action on the Vogtle COLs under 10 C.F.R. § 2.206, asking the NRC to require Vogtle
Facility licensees to conduct safety analyses of severe accident scenarios in which the
44
AP1000 hydrogen igniter system would be actuated too late. To date, the NRC has not yet
made a determination whether this request is proper under § 2.206. No formal response from
SNC will be due unless and until the NRC determines that the request will be considered.

13. The status of transportation links for heavy forgings and modules.
Forging activities have been completed and all required forgings have been transported for
major components to begin fabrication. Fabrication of equipment from these forgings is
progressing on schedule and deliveries of all major components are scheduled to meet
construction need dates. No additional heavy forgings were transported to manufacturing
facilities during the reporting period.
Ten structural sub-modules were transported by truck from the SMS facility to the Facility
site during the reporting period.
14. An updated comparison of the economics of the certified project to other capacity
options.
The Company’s economic analysis continues to indicate that the Facility remains
economically beneficial for customers as compared with another generation alternative.
While the Company’s methodologies and assumptions utilized in its economic analyses
differ from those of Public Interest Advocacy Staff Witness, Phil Hayet, Mr. Hayet’s own
analyses has consistently shown that the project can incur significant capital cost increases
before it would become uneconomic for customers.
The relative economic value for the Facility can be determined by comparing the costs
associated with completing, operating, and maintaining the Facility over its expected 60 year
useful life with the costs to build, operate, and maintain a combined cycle (“CC”) natural gas
alternative, which is the next most viable generation alternative, over a comparable time
period. The economic analysis performed for this Seventh VCM Report has relied on the
methodologies used in all previous economic evaluations conducted in Docket Nos. 27800
and 29849.
45
The economic evaluation presented in this Seventh VCM Report is based on the same
underlying major planning assumptions used in the Sixth VCM Report. Consistent with the
original certification filing and all previous semi-annual VCM reports, a range of planning
scenarios was used to evaluate the possible impacts of varying fuel prices and carbon costs.
Three possible fuel price forecasts were used along with three possible carbon cost scenarios.
The fuel forecasts are based on the Company’s B2012 fuel forecasts. The carbon cost
scenarios start in 2015 with costs of $0 (existing), $10 (moderate), and $20 (substantial) and
include escalation.
The estimate of the capital cost to complete and the in-service dates of the Facility has been
updated from the Sixth VCM Report along with pre-COD Operations and Maintenance
(“O&M”), post-COD O&M for the Facility, projected post-COD ongoing capital additions,
and nuclear fuel. The in-service dates of the gas-fired CC units have been updated from the
Sixth VCM Report to be consistent with the new in-service dates of the Facility.
Decommissioning costs, spent fuel storage cost estimates, and the assumed operating
characteristics of the Facility have not changed. The long-term marginal financing rates for
debt and preferred stock have been updated to reflect current expectations. It should be noted
that these marginal financing costs are higher than the current estimate of embedded average
financing costs, which are used in all other references to financing costs in this report.
Consistent with the Sixth VCM Report, the current economic evaluation assumes 50 percent
of potentially available PTCs. Finally, this economic analysis continues to exclude the
expected benefits of the DOE loan guarantee even though the Company expects net savings
to customers resulting from the program.
“Sunk costs” (non-refundable capital and financing costs already incurred or projected to
have been incurred as of August 31, 2012) are excluded from this forward-looking analysis.
The current forecast of construction and capital costs as shown in Table 1.1, net of sunk
costs, is used as the basis to determine “cost to complete.”
The relative economics for the Facility, when compared to the gas-fired CC alternative, vary
depending on the assumptions for future fuel prices as well as with the projected carbon costs
associated with potential future carbon regulation. Table 14.1 below shows the difference
between the lifetime costs of building, operating, and maintaining the gas-fired CC
alternative and the Facility, with positive savings meaning the Facility is less expensive to
customers than the gas-fired CC alternative. All nine scenarios show positive benefits to
customers for completing and operating the Facility.
46

Positive number means the Facility is less costly than the gas-fired CC
alternative.
The Company continues to believe equal weighting of these scenario outcomes is most
appropriate given the difficulty in assessing the outcome of a vast range of key variables such
as future environmental regulations, possible climate change regulation, fuel prices, demand
levels, potential federal portfolio requirements, federal policies toward new nuclear, the
breadth and rate of expansion of new nuclear in the United States, and the interplay of other
market forces. As such, the weighted average expected value of the relative savings for
completion of the Facility as compared to the gas-fired CC alternative is $5.4 billion based
on the results provided in Table 14.1.
Alternatively, the results of the updated economic evaluation can be expressed in terms of the
“breakeven capital cost to complete.” Table 14.2 below shows the results of the breakeven
analysis that calculates the maximum capital expenditure that could be spent to complete the
Facility and maintain lifetime costs that are equal to the cost of the gas-fired CC alternative.
In all of the scenarios, the maximum capital cost to complete the Facility exceeds the
Company’s current estimate of the cost to complete the Facility (including marginal
construction financing costs) of $3.2 billion.

that the cost to complete the Facility could increase by $4.1 billion over
the current estimated cost to complete the Facility before becoming
uneconomic. (This value can be derived by averaging the results from the
nine scenarios above and then subtracting the current estimated cost to
complete).
The analyses provided in Tables 14.1 and 14.2 are based on an economic assessment from an
“incremental cost to complete” perspective, which ignores any potential cancellation fees or
other costs that would be incurred if the project were stopped, as well as any fully-committed
construction costs that would not be avoidable in the event the project is cancelled. If the
results from the incremental cost to complete evaluation showed it was no longer cost-
effective to pursue completing the Facility, a second cancellation assessment would be
performed to determine the economic value of canceling the Facility. A cancellation
assessment can provide the most appropriate perspective for deciding whether to cancel the
Facility as it would include the impacts of any cancellation fees or other costs associated with
cancelling the Facility in the economic analysis. However, because Tables 14.1 and 14.2 both
reflect significant savings and benefits to customers from the incremental cost to complete
perspective across a wide range of possible future fuel and carbon prices, a cancellation
assessment is not warranted at this time.
Per the final order from the Sixth VCM Report, the Company agreed to provide scenario
studies for comparison purposes to the results provided in Table 14.2 in which the in-service
dates are delayed by 12 months and 18 months from April 2016 and April 2017 for units 3
and 4, respectively. These scenarios include additional capital costs and financing costs
related to potential delays and the results are provided in Table 14.3 and 14.4.

In summary, all scenario studies indicate that the Facility would remain economic despite the
additional costs associated with a potential 12 month or 18 month delay from the originally
contemplated CODs. In both potential delay scenarios, the Facility remains less costly than
the next best fuel alternative and will continue to benefit customers. These scenarios do not
represent the Company’s projection for the ultimate outcome of the project but instead
provide context regarding the economic viability of the Facility considering reasonably
possible delay circumstances.
